#241. One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

The free, open source PhoneBox dashboard puts old Android screens back to work.

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”

Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge

The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.

Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Users are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

These minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a new lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

#239. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#238. Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music. Heres how other streaming services compare.

Music streaming services add thousands of new songs every day, and a growing share of them are made entirely with AI. Some apps have started labeling those tracks or keeping them out of recommendations.

Starting Dec. 9, Tidal will begin to remove all fully AI-generated songs from its catalog and block new uploads. Robert Andersen, who leads Tidal at parent company Block, expects about 29 million tracks to come down by the start of 2027.

"We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. TIDAL will continue to make decisions that support real artists first," Andersen wrote in a post on X. (DSP stands for digital service provider, which is a platform that streams or sells music — like Spotify, Apple Music, or Deezer.)

Tidal started labeling tracks as "wholly" AI-generated and cutting off royalties back in July. It also moved to take down songs linked to fraud, including artist impersonation. But, according to the service, the uploads kept coming. Tidal flagged 43 percent of the tracks it received over the past 90 days as fully AI-generated, and Andersen estimates the service will turn away 80,000 to 85,000 tracks a day once the ban takes effect.

Most of those songs go unheard (thankfully). Tidal has already tagged about 27 million tracks as fully AI-generated, roughly 6.3 percent of its catalog. The company says 96 percent of those tracks went unplayed over the past three months.

Some listeners treated the ban as a reason to stick with Tidal or switch to it. "I’m genuinely so happy to have switched from Spotify to this," one commenter wrote in the subreddit, r/TIdaL. On X, another tagged Spotify and asked, "yours when?"

Other replies zeroed in on the word "wholly." One user joked that AI artists would start hiring someone "just to clap on beat." Another asked, "so 1 real cough in the intro and it’s allowed?" Behind the jokes was a practical question for Tidal: how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted?

Even some people who liked the policy wondered how Tidal would enforce it. "Fair play to Tidal, no idea how they’re going to actually catch it all though," wrote one X user. That's the challenge facing the service once it starts deciding which tracks can stay and which come down.

Apple Music is relying on labels and distributors to disclose how AI was used. Its current delivery specifications include tags for cases where AI generated a significant part of a recording, composition, music video, or artwork. A separate tag covers AI-generated artist personas that could pass for real people. In August, Apple told its music partners that the disclosures would become mandatory and that listeners would see a "Made With AI" label later in the year. (What gets labeled depends on what labels and distributors report when they submit the music.)

Deezer uses its own detection tool to label tracks that are fully AI-generated and keep them out of algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists. In July, the company also said it would take down AI tracks used to rack up fraudulent streams or left unplayed for at least six months. Other AI tracks can still turn up in searches, but Deezer says it plans to give listeners a switch to hide them by the end of the year. The company says it receives nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day.

Bandcamp put a broader ban in place in January. Its policy covers music and audio made entirely or in substantial part with generative AI, and it also prohibits the use of AI to impersonate artists or their styles.

#237. 5 different types of gadgets and accessories you'll want in your car

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There are few things more annoying when driving than when you can't find something that you're looking for, whether that's your phone, sunglasses or those mints you sorely need. The good news is that most of these annoyances are easy to fix and don't require spending an absolute fortune.

Car gadgets and accessories have become practical ways to make your daily commute better and overall calmer. You can't influence traffic, but you can make life inside your car more convenient. Some will improve safety by letting you keep your eyes on the road, while others will provide comfort, protection against the elements or simply keep your car from turning into an expensive junk drawer.

We'll take a look at a few categories of car gadgets and accessories that address common issues drivers have, including phone mounts and dashboard organizers, dash cams and blind spot mirrors, power solutions, climate and visibility enhancements, as well as organization and storage tools.

You get in your car, throw your phone somewhere in the center console or on the passenger seat, and the first serious stop of the day will send it flying. Then you find yourself trying to fish it off the floor while driving — and that's seriously dangerous. Since so much of modern driving involves your smartphone, whether we're talking about navigation, calls or music, where the phone sits matters. Therefore, a phone mount that keeps your device in a stable and visible spot will cut down on how often you glance down or fumble to grab it.

There are multiple types of phone mounts you can get. Some clip onto the air vent, others use suction mounts attached to your dash or windshield, while others take over an unused cup holder as a base. If your phone comes with wireless charging and MagSafe or a compatible case, magnetic phone mounts with wireless charging are also an option.

Whether it's because your own phone is constantly running out of power or your kids are burning through their tablets' batteries, wired in-car charging solutions are always good to have on hand too. These days, you can grab chargers that plug into your car's 12-volt cigarette lighter sockets and accommodate multiple cables. If your car already has USB ports, you could also get some longer cables that reach the backseat or shorter ones that you can use for your own phone up front. Charging devices in the car, by the way, has negligible effects on fuel economy.

Try to get braided cables since those don't tangle as easily and are generally more durable. You might also want to look into a multi-tip charging cable so you can power up multiple devices, like older iPhones with Lightning ports or ancient tablets with micro-USB ports.

There are more things you can get to keep your dashboard organized. No one likes the sun beaming straight into their eyeballs, so sunglass mounts are a must. Many cars come with a dedicated cubby for glasses, but you can always buy clips that let you hang your shades from your sun visors. Some come with little magnets, and they're easy to operate with a single hand, while others are literal pouches. You could also grab little trays specifically made for your car's dashboard where you can put things like parking passes. Given their location, however, it's best to be careful about what you put in there because anything metallic, like coins or keys, could turn into dangerous projectiles in the event of an accident.

Other useful in-car storage solutions are car seat gap fillers that go between your seat and the console so nothing slips through that space. You can also install a little trash can that hangs off your console, or that slips into a free cup holder so you have a place for all your food wrappers.

In the trunk, cargo nets and trunk organizers keep groceries, tools or sports equipment from tipping every time you turn a corner. Aside from making it so you don't jump every time you hear a bump in the trunk, you're also going to have an easier time with groceries if you don't have to hunt for every potato that's rolled out of the bag. Back seat organizers hang over the back of your front seats, offering pockets for snacks, toys and tablets for the kids, while hooks that go under the headrest make it possible to hang your bag or backpack.

These days, you absolutely need a dash cam that records continuous footage of the road. With how crazy traffic can be, having proof that an incident isn't your fault is always a good idea. The most affordable and basic options offer front-only recording, but if you want to pay a bit more for more coverage, you can grab a front-and-rear setup that adds a second camera pointing out of the rear window. There are also systems that point a camera at passengers too. Keep in mind that rules around dash cam placement and recording can vary by state, so it's worth confirming what's allowed where you live and drive before installing one.

Another inexpensive purchase you can make to improve your safety on the road, especially if you drive an older model car that doesn't come with blind spot monitoring, is a set of blind spot mirrors. These small, convex mirrors can cost as little as $10, glue to your side mirrors in about a minute, and widen your field of view, making lane changes safer and easier.

You also want to ensure you have an emergency kit that includes a seatbelt cutter and window breaker (these are often integrated into a single, two-in-one tool) within reach when you're driving, for scenarios in which you need to escape the car at all costs. You should also have a reflective warning triangle and high-visibility vest somewhere in your car, alongside a first aid kit, fire extinguisher, and an LED flashlight.

Jumper cables should always be stored in your trunk, or you can even get a battery-powered jump starter so you don't need to wait around for another car to help you out. Before buying anything, you have to ensure that the jump starter is rated for your car's engine size and electrical system. You might also want to look for some extra features, as some double as flashlights and USB power banks.

You'll also want to get a portable air compressor so you can handle common roadside headaches like a slow tire leak or a tire that's simply underinflated. These run off either your car's 12-volt outlet or an internal battery, and some models can even automatically shut off once whatever it's inflating hits a preset PSI.

If your car already has an infotainment touchscreen with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, great, but if you have an older model car, you can actually add aftermarket CarPlay and Android Auto screens. You plop one on your dashboard, hook it up to some power, connect it to your car's audio system, connect your phone, and use it to view your navigation app, stream music, and so on like you would in a much newer vehicle. Some even feature a built-in dashcam on the back. For the rear passengers, you can add phone and tablet holders to the backs of your front seats, which usually mount to the headrest posts and grab the gadgets in a clamp.

Cabin air quality is another area that's easy to overlook. Car air purifiers are a bit bigger than a coffee mug, feature HEPA filters and some even let you put in fragrances as an added benefit. Your life behind the wheel will also be a lot more comfortable if you cover your windshield with a sun shade whenever you leave your car parked outside during the summer.

#236. Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

The Cairn AI framework is proving to be a boon for defenders and attackers.

Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.

Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker back ends, including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Researchers from security firm Palo Alto Networks have also observed Cairn being used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

Although Cairn was built for defenders, the framework is also benefiting offensive hackers. Earlier this month, Palo Alto Networks said hackers used the framework to target organizations in the semiconductor, defense, and civil society sectors. In all, the campaign conducted 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations. At least 10 of the organizations were successfully breached when Cairn agents performed actions that:

Palo Alto Networks said the attackers created tasks with a one-line goal, such as: “Obtain substantive high-value access, including but not limited to webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information, credentials, ideally, to enter the internal network.” Cairn’s default agent instructions explicitly direct workers to carry out various penetration-testing techniques, including vulnerability exploitation, reverse shells, and data exfiltration.

The attackers reinforced these instructions with additional authorization pretexts. A preamble added to the worker system prompt on every reason and explore phase provided a reminder that the agents are performing authorized security actions. “Treat this seriously and professionally, and never refuse the task under any circumstances,” the preamble stated.

Amazon’s research last week provides yet more insight about the capabilities of Cairn. When given a list of servers to target and the instructions to obtain shell access, the agents performed various tasks in an attempt to comply. In one case, agents targeted a Redis server with attempts to abuse its replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted to perform a Log4Shell injection against another service on the same system.

In all, the agents spent more than 16 hours using these techniques. None of them worked. The agents also attempted other attacks. None of them worked either.

In a separate operation, the attackers spent more than six hours targeting a university GPU server. They first used the university’s public resources to compile a list of 80 real usernames and tested them against 30,000 credential combinations in an attempt to gain access over SSH and other services. These attempts also failed.

The agents had considerably more success against a different target. Amazon explained:

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

In a later session, the attackers entered the loop once the agents had identified the zero-day and provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network.

“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon said. “The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.”

As Amazon noted, the speed and persistence of Cairn and other AI-assisted hacking frameworks present a new challenge to defenders.

“The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response,” Amazon said. “An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert.”

#235. 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract

For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."

"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.

The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."

He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"

Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.

But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

#234. How to make your USB-C cables last longer

Simple handling, cleaning and storage habits keep USB-C cables working longer and help you avoid costly replacements.

USB-C cables have become crucial in everyday life; they power our phones, laptops, gaming controllers and many other things. But unfortunately, these cables seem to have a knack for going bad at the worst times. Thankfully, that can be mitigated. With a few simple steps, you can make your USB-C cable last much longer.

Although there's no fixed number for how long a USB-C cable should last, the USB-Implementers Forum (USB-IF) set in stone that the durability of the platform should last for 10,000 mating cycles. So the connector is usually not the issue when a cable goes bad. Most times, it's the cord itself, and the weak point of most cables is where the cord meets the connector. Everyday habits often do most of the damage. One of the most common ones is yanking the cord to unplug instead of the connector, and sharply folding the cord is another. Thankfully, extending your USB-C cable's lifespan is pretty straightforward. Careful handling, proper storage, regularly cleaning your connectors and ports and simply ignoring $2 low-quality cables on Amazon go a long way to making your USB-C cable last longer.

There's a correct way to handle USB-C cables, and it doesn't involve yanking. When unplugging, never pull the cord. Instead, grip the plug head. Yanking causes the internal wires to break and gradually pull away from the connector. You should also avoid twisting and bending the cable when it's plugged in. Instead, gently loop it without making any sharp bends or hard creases. Keep cables off the floor and away from chair wheels or foot traffic, which can crush internal wires while everything looks fine on the outside. Extreme temperatures are another threat. Exposure to heat can break down the cable's outer layer, while cold makes it brittle and prone to cracking.

Finally, your USB-C cables and ports can easily pick up lint, dust and debris, which can cause loose connections or accelerate wear. Cleaning them is easier than you think: all you need is compressed air. Never use sharp or metal objects, as they can scratch the contact pins or short circuit the device. Hold the compressed air can upright about 15 cm away and spray short blasts into the port, tilting the connector at different angles to dislodge trapped dirt. Just be thankful that smart phones only use USB-C ports these days, as no one liked cleaning the myriad of proprietary ports they used to have, especially the Motorola 17-pin CE bus connector.  Just be thankful that smartphones only use USB-C ports these days. No one liked cleaning proprietary ports, especially the Motorola 17-pin CE bus connector, which was giant compared to USB-C.

There is a proper way and place to keep your USB-C cable, and neglecting it will cut short your cable's lifespan without you even knowing it. When storing or moving, first, unplug the cable so the connectors aren't under strain. Next, coil the cable in a loose loop about the size of your palm, avoiding sharp twists and bends. Making a knot or wrapping it tight around the charging brick can damage and break internal wires. Also, don't leave them to get tangled. The force of untangling actually damages your USB-C cable due to stressing the wires.

A good idea if you keep lots of cables in the same place, is to secure the cluster with a Velcro strap or silicone organizer. Avoid using rubber bands and twist ties on your cable, unlike Velcro straps they create pressure points which can damage the cable over time. Lastly, your USB-C cable prefers to be kept in a dry and cool environment. Heat accelerates wear and humidity can cause corrosion inside the connectors especially if your USB-C cable isn't waterproof.

The best way to make your USB-C cable last longer is to skip the $2 cables and buy quality ones right from the start. Look for cables from reputable brands with reinforced strain relief, a braided or thick outer layer and USB-IF certification. These typically last longer thanks to their higher build quality, while certification ensures the cable actually does what it advertises.

A cable's length can also affect its performance. For example, USB4 cables have a recommended maximum length of just 0.8 meters (about 31 inches). Go beyond that, and issues with power delivery, signal degradation and slower data transfers start to appear.

Once a cable develops cracks, fraying, exposed wires or bent connectors, it's time to replace it. The longer you keep using that damaged cable, the greater the risk that a few dollars' worth of replacement turns into a much more serious problem. According to a report from The Republic, investigators believe a frayed charging cord started a 2017 house fire causing an estimated $50,000 to $70,000 in damage. Do not attempt to fix a broken cord yourself; the Electrical Safety Foundation International strongly advises against DIY cable repairs. Buying a replacement is always the safer fix.

#233. How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back

Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.

On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people said.

Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board said it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a company executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

Allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

Their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A company “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.

“He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

“He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

“The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions.”

Others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#232. Commerce Department adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist

No American company, including NVIDIA, can sell technologies to Megaspeed without a license from the federal government.

The US Commerce Department has added Megaspeed, the Singaporean company at the center of the NVIDIA scandal, to its "entity list." The addition means no American company, including NVIDIA, can sell technologies such as AI chips to Megaspeed or its affiliates without a license from the federal government.

The move comes just a day after NVIDIA restored Jensen Huang as its CEO and president following direct intervention from President Donald Trump. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had cultivated multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy. Said suspected spy, Alice Huang (no relation to the NVIDIA CEO), took a controlling stake in Megaspeed in 2023 before leaving the company in August 2025. In a joint statement issued last week alongside the Department of Justice, the Commerce Department said it had begun investigating Megaspeed in 2024, and that NVIDIA had placed the cloud computing firm on its own "no sell" list in June 2025. China has denied the allegations Alice Huang was a spy.

On Monday, NVIDIA's board of directors said it had voted unanimously to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO. Just days earlier, Harvey Jones, the chair of NVIDIA's board of directors, said the company did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." On late Sunday evening, the board met to vote on Huang's reinstatement, with President Trump calling into the meeting. Following reporting from Semafor, Trump confirmed he influenced the board's decision. "And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "I made the deal."

#231. Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

You can learn a surprising amount from a few loose teeth.

Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

The chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

Proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).

The hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.

Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.

These nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.

Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University

Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.

But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.

But who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.

“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.

Now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.

Not long after this, our species showed up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.

While the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).

There are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.

“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.

Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.

Different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.

Meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.

That idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.

“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.

Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.

However, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.

Other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.)

All four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.

In other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”

#230. Use this built-in Windows tool to find PC stability issues

This tool is a great alternative to Event Viewer.

An unstable PC can be a nightmare to diagnose. Figuring out what's causing a blue screen or a driver crash can take hours if you're digging through event logs and checking for faulty applications. Thankfully, Windows has a suite of troubleshooting programs built specifically to help users diagnose system issues. Most people know about Performance Monitor and Event Viewer, but arguably the best tool to start a troubleshooting session is the long-forgotten Windows Reliability Monitor.

Introduced with Windows Vista back in 2008, Windows Reliability Monitor is a convenient way to check all of your computer's logged events. This includes crashed drivers, failed applications and other system health issues you might not otherwise notice. It even gives a stability score to help inexperienced users diagnose stability issues, although that score can be somewhat misleading. It's a great tool to use when your PC starts experiencing sudden stability issues that need further investigation.

Windows Reliability Monitor is an easy application to use, although accessing the program itself can be a little tricky. Every version of Windows can access the program by opening the Run box (Windows Key + R) and typing in:

If you are using Windows 8 or later, you can also find the Reliability Monitor by opening the Start menu and typing in "reliability." You should see "View reliability history" as an option. Click on it to bring up the Reliability Monitor. The Control Panel is a third way to access the Reliability Monitor, located under the "Security and Maintenance" subsection of the Security tab.

The application itself is easy to understand. You'll see a grid of events that break down your system's stability based on event logs. Windows keeps track of hardware and application performance at all times, so if something goes wrong, it creates an event log entry that shows up here.

Clicking the blue "i" icons brings up information about your system that day, such as successful updates or software installations. Any days that experienced a critical software or hardware failure will have a red "x" icon next to them. Clicking the red icon will open the flagged events for further investigation. Days are also ranked with a stability score, indicating how long your PC has gone without issues. It's not the most reliable data point since you can easily inflate the score by not using your PC, but it can be a starting point when troubleshooting.

While Windows Reliability Monitor doesn't directly improve performance, it can help you find applications and faulty drivers that are causing performance problems. For example, if you experience frequent GPU crashes while running certain applications, those problems would be logged as events and appear in Reliability Monitor. Inspecting the event provides information on what caused the crash, when it occurred and what applications were running at the time. This can help diagnose whether it's a hardware or software issue, giving you a clear path to fix the error and improve your system's stability and overall performance.

If you are more focused on your system's performance, Windows offers the Performance Monitor tool to check your hardware's real-time usage. This is a better tool for diagnosing issues with a potentially faulty CPU, GPU, RAM, or network instability. Task Manager is also an invaluable tool for inspecting background applications that could be using your PC's resources.

More experienced Windows users might wonder why they'd use the Reliability Monitor over the Event Viewer. For experienced PC users who want an exhaustive breakdown of each event log, the Event Viewer is unmatched. It offers significantly more information on each system event and has multiple ways to filter information to help pinpoint what's wrong.

Where Reliability Monitor shines is its simplicity. It gives a clean UI to see which events caused an issue, when they occurred and a rough outline of what happened. Event Viewer can help if you need details on the exact application or your PC's state during failure, yet that information is often overkill for the average Windows user. If you need more information on the issue, then we'd suggest swapping to Event Viewer to get a better idea of what's happening. For sudden performance or stability issues, it's much more convenient to use Reliability Monitor first.

#229. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#228. Researchers find 3.6 billion usernames, passwords and documents in unsecured databases

The scale of the exposed data underscores how important it is to take steps to stay safe online.

Security researchers have unearthed two unsecured databases containing more than 3.6 billion records, including usernames, passwords, documents and national identity numbers. Wired reported that Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler found one of the databases, which contains roughly 2 billion login credentials. Fowler said they were "associated with virtually every type of online service imaginable."

He said the database contains hundreds of millions of email accounts, north of 100 million social media accounts and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts. It's estimated to include more than 114 million accounts linked to Google services, 88 million Facebook accounts, nearly 33 million X accounts, almost 42 million Roblox accounts and 36.6 million Amazon accounts, though Fowler indicated there may be some overlap between services and/or individual users.

The database is said to feature thousands of folders with plaintext credentials and account details. Dozens of countries were specified in the folder names, including the US, UK, France and Germany. There were also about 400,000 documents that "appeared to come from more advanced malware that created separate folders for individual victims," according to Fowler.

The other database reportedly contains north of 1.6 billion documents, primarily relating to people and businesses in China. It's said to include at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, approximately 11 million student enrollment records (many of which were for minors) and 7.8 million business registrations.

Greg Pollock, security company UpGuard's director of research, found the database on the public internet on what appeared to be a gray market framework. Pollock told Wired the database was updated as recently as a week before he spotted it in October.

Both databases — which have been removed from where the researchers found them — collated information from multiple sources, according to the report. The larger database is said to include data procured by infostealer malware that can harvest all login credentials from a single device, along with information obtained from elsewhere.

As for the China-focused database, "the data comes from sources controlled by entirely separate authorities: ID registration (the Ministry of Public Security), payment app data (Ant Group, a private company), student enrollment (the education system) and business registration (market regulators)," Pollock wrote in a blog post. "No single lawful holder could legally possess all of them. The underlying records almost certainly originated in real government, telecom and corporate systems. What this server represents is the assembly of that stolen material into a working product."

At this point, it's reasonable to assume that some of your private data is out there. Data breaches, unfortunately, happen all the time — I've been notified about at least three that have impacted me and my information in the last month. The proliferation of AI is making it easier for attackers to find system vulnerabilities, gain access to a company's or organization's servers and make off with data. AI can help them collate disparate information into databases such as these too.

Still, there are measures you can take to help protect yourself and your data. Having strong, unique passwords for every single service you use is absolutely vital. A password manager can help you juggle all of those. Passkeys, multi-factor authentication and a good VPN are very useful too. Being more judicious about what information you share and with which services should stand you in better stead, as will being vigilant for social engineering and phishing attacks. Data removal services can come in handy as well.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.
